subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity
intro: Strong readers can read and understand many kinds of informational text, from history and science to biography and current events. Comprehension means more than reading the words. It means finding the main idea, picking out key details, drawing inferences, and understanding how the parts of a text fit together. This lesson gives you practice reading grade-level nonfiction and answering questions about what you read.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The octopus is one of the most intelligent animals in the ocean. It has eight arms lined with sensitive suckers that can taste and grip at the same time. An octopus can change the color and texture of its skin in an instant, allowing it to blend into rocks, coral, or sand to hide from predators. Some octopuses even squeeze through tiny cracks barely larger than their eyes, since their soft bodies have no bones. Scientists have watched octopuses solve puzzles, open jars, and use shells as shelter, behaviors that show real problem-solving ability.

What is the main idea of this passage?

steps: Read the whole passage and ask what it is mostly about.
Notice that every sentence describes a special ability of the octopus, such as camouflage, squeezing through cracks, and solving puzzles.
The first sentence states the main point directly: the octopus is highly intelligent.
Combine the details to confirm that the passage is about how remarkable and intelligent the octopus is.
solution.answer: The main idea is that the octopus is a highly intelligent and remarkable ocean animal. The passage supports this by describing its sensitive arms, its ability to change color and texture, its boneless body that squeezes through tiny cracks, and its problem-solving behaviors like opening jars and using shells as shelter.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

In 1955, a woman named Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama. At the time, laws forced Black Americans to sit in the back of buses and give up their seats when white passengers wanted them. Parks's quiet act of resistance led to her arrest, but it also sparked a year-long bus boycott in which Black residents refused to ride the buses. The boycott drew national attention and helped launch the larger civil rights movement. Rosa Parks became a lasting symbol of courage and the fight for equal rights.

Why is Rosa Parks's action described as important?

steps: Identify what Rosa Parks did: she refused to give up her bus seat.
Find the effects the passage describes: her arrest, a year-long bus boycott, national attention, and help launching the civil rights movement.
Connect the action to its results to see why it mattered.
Conclude that her action is important because of the large movement it helped start.
solution.answer: Rosa Parks's action is described as important because it did more than affect one bus ride. Her refusal led to her arrest and sparked a year-long bus boycott that drew national attention and helped launch the larger civil rights movement. Because one quiet act of resistance helped begin a major fight for equal rights, the passage presents her as a lasting symbol of courage.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Glaciers are huge masses of ice that form over many years as snow piles up and presses together. They move very slowly, sometimes only a few inches a day, but over long periods they can carve valleys, shape mountains, and move enormous boulders. Glaciers store much of the world's fresh water in frozen form. In recent decades, many glaciers have been shrinking as temperatures rise. Scientists study glaciers closely because their melting can raise sea levels and affect the supply of fresh water for people who live downstream.

What can you infer about why scientists are concerned about shrinking glaciers?

steps: The question asks for an inference, so combine clues rather than copying one sentence.
Note that glaciers store much of the world's fresh water and that their melting can raise sea levels.
Note that people downstream depend on glaciers for fresh water.
Put these clues together to infer the concern: melting glaciers threaten both water supplies and coastlines.
solution.answer: You can infer that scientists are concerned because shrinking glaciers threaten two important things. First, glaciers store much of the world's fresh water, so their melting could reduce the water supply for people who live downstream. Second, the melted water raises sea levels, which can endanger coastlines. By combining these clues, you can infer that the concern is about both losing fresh water and rising seas.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The ancient city of Pompeii was buried in volcanic ash when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. While the eruption was a disaster, the thick ash actually preserved the city in remarkable detail. When archaeologists uncovered Pompeii centuries later, they found streets, homes, shops, paintings, and even the shapes of people frozen in their final moments. These discoveries gave historians an extraordinary look at daily life in the Roman world. Pompeii remains one of the most important archaeological sites ever found.

The passage says the eruption was a disaster but also had an unexpected result. What was that result?

steps: Find the contrast signal in the passage: 'While the eruption was a disaster.'
Read what follows to find the unexpected positive result.
The passage says the thick ash preserved the city in remarkable detail.
Confirm the result by noting what archaeologists later found and learned.
solution.answer: The unexpected result was that the thick volcanic ash preserved the city of Pompeii in remarkable detail. Although the eruption was a disaster, the ash protected streets, homes, shops, and paintings, so that when archaeologists uncovered the city centuries later, they could learn an extraordinary amount about daily life in the Roman world.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some types can grow more than three feet in a single day. Although it looks like a tree, bamboo is actually a kind of grass. People around the world use bamboo for building houses, making furniture, and even creating cloth and paper. Because it grows so quickly and can be harvested without killing the plant, bamboo is considered an environmentally friendly material. Pandas also depend on bamboo, eating it for nearly all of their meals.

Why does the passage call bamboo an environmentally friendly material?

steps: Locate the sentence that mentions bamboo being environmentally friendly.
Read the reason given in that sentence.
The passage says bamboo grows quickly and can be harvested without killing the plant.
Explain how these traits make it friendly to the environment.
solution.answer: The passage calls bamboo environmentally friendly because it grows very quickly and can be harvested without killing the plant. This means people can use bamboo again and again without using it up, unlike materials that require cutting down trees that take many years to grow back. Its fast growth and renewable nature make it a more sustainable choice.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The Sahara Desert was not always a sea of sand. Thousands of years ago, parts of it were green, with lakes, rivers, and grasslands where animals grazed. Ancient rock paintings found in the desert show people swimming and hunting animals that need plenty of water, such as hippos. Over time, the climate slowly changed, rainfall decreased, and the region dried into the vast desert we know today. Scientists study these changes to understand how climates shift over long periods.

What is the main idea of this passage?
items.hint: Look for the big point that all the details support, not just one fact.

steps: Read the passage and ask what it is mostly about.
Notice that the details describe how the Sahara changed from green land to desert.
The main idea is the transformation of the Sahara over time.
Confirm with the supporting evidence about rock paintings and changing climate.
solution.answer: The main idea is that the Sahara Desert was once a green region and slowly changed into a desert over thousands of years. The passage supports this with details such as ancient rock paintings showing people swimming and hunting water-loving animals, and the explanation that rainfall decreased and the climate dried out over time.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The heart is a powerful muscle about the size of a fist. It beats around 100,000 times a day, pumping blood through a vast network of vessels to deliver oxygen and nutrients to every part of the body. The blood then returns to the heart to be sent to the lungs, where it picks up fresh oxygen. This cycle repeats every minute of every day, without rest, for a person's entire life. Keeping the heart healthy through exercise and good food helps it do its important job.

According to the passage, what happens to blood after it returns to the heart?
items.hint: Find the sentence that describes where the blood goes after coming back to the heart.

steps: Locate the part of the passage about blood returning to the heart.
Read what the passage says happens next.
The blood is sent to the lungs to pick up fresh oxygen.
State the answer clearly using that detail.
solution.answer: According to the passage, after blood returns to the heart, it is sent to the lungs, where it picks up fresh oxygen. Then the cycle repeats as the heart pumps the oxygen-rich blood back out to the body.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

For centuries, sailors navigated the oceans using the stars, the sun, and simple tools. One of the most important tools was the compass, which always points toward magnetic north. With a compass, sailors could keep a steady direction even when clouds hid the sky or land was nowhere in sight. The invention of the compass made long sea voyages safer and helped explorers travel farther than ever before. Today, ships use satellites and computers, but the compass remains a reliable backup.

Why was the compass so important to early sailors? Use the passage to support your answer.
items.hint: Think about what the compass let sailors do that they could not do as easily before.

steps: Find what the passage says the compass does: it always points toward magnetic north.
Find why that mattered: sailors could keep a steady direction even when clouds hid the sky or land was out of sight.
Connect this ability to the results described, such as safer voyages and farther exploration.
Write an answer that links the tool to its benefit.
solution.answer: The compass was so important because it always points toward magnetic north, which let sailors keep a steady direction even when clouds hid the sky or no land was in sight. According to the passage, this made long sea voyages safer and helped explorers travel farther than ever before, since they no longer had to rely only on the stars and sun.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The Internet began as a small project in the 1960s that connected a few university computers so researchers could share information. Over the following decades, it grew into a worldwide network linking billions of devices. Today the Internet shapes how people communicate, learn, shop, and work. It allows information to travel across the globe in seconds. However, the Internet also raises new challenges, such as protecting personal privacy and deciding which information online can be trusted.

What can you infer about how much the Internet has changed since the 1960s?
items.hint: Compare what the Internet was at the start with what it is described as today.

steps: Find what the Internet was in the 1960s: a small project connecting a few university computers.
Find what it is today: a worldwide network linking billions of devices that shapes daily life.
Compare the two to make an inference about the scale of change.
State the inference clearly.
solution.answer: You can infer that the Internet has changed enormously since the 1960s. It began as a small project connecting just a few university computers, but it has grown into a worldwide network linking billions of devices that now shapes how people communicate, learn, shop, and work. The huge difference between its small start and its global reach today shows just how dramatic the change has been.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Many birds build nests to protect their eggs and young. Different species build very different kinds of nests. Some weave tiny cup-shaped nests from grass and twigs, while others dig burrows in the ground or hollow out holes in trees. The bald eagle builds one of the largest nests of any bird, sometimes weighing over a ton and used again year after year. No matter the size or shape, a nest serves the same purpose: keeping eggs and chicks safe and warm until they are ready to survive on their own.

What is the main point the author makes about bird nests, even though nests can be very different?
items.hint: Look at the last sentence, which ties all the examples together.

steps: Notice the passage gives many examples of different nests.
Look for the sentence that connects all the examples.
The last sentence says that no matter the size or shape, a nest serves the same purpose.
State the unifying main point.
solution.answer: The author's main point is that even though bird nests come in many different sizes and shapes, they all serve the same purpose: keeping eggs and chicks safe and warm until the young birds are ready to survive on their own. The various examples, from tiny woven cups to the bald eagle's huge nest, all support this shared idea.
